content.title: About
content.content: Channa Saag is a traditional Indian dish made from spinach leaves (saag) and chickpeas (channa), seasoned with spices, ginger, garlic and tomato sauce. The dish is rich in plant protein, fiber and B‑vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is called "saag" in Indian cuisine and appears in hundreds of recipes.
Chickpeas are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown for more than 7,000 years.
Channa Saag is commonly served with Indian flatbreads (naan, roti) or rice.
The dish is popular among vegetarians because it provides a complete amino‑acid profile.
Traditional recipes often include mustard seeds and fenugreek for extra aroma.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas deliver about 20 g of protein per 100 g, important for vegetarian diets.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Spinach provides iron, calcium, magnesium and vitamin K, while chickpeas are high in folate and vitamin B6.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The dish raises blood sugar slowly, making it suitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Spinach contains carotenoids and lutein that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chickpeas.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Large amounts of spinach can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If prepared with a lot of salt, the dish may be unsuitable for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Channa Saag hot, typically with Indian flatbread (naan, roti) or boiled rice. A squeeze of lime or a dollop of yogurt adds freshness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Low‑fat cottage cheese with low sodium is a dairy product made from skimmed milk that has been curdled and drained of whey. It has a soft, creamy texture, a mildly tangy flavor, and contains minimal fat and salt, making it suitable for diet‑focused eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is one of the oldest dairy foods, with evidence of its production in ancient Egypt.
Low‑fat versions are popular in fitness circles for high‑protein, low‑calorie meals.
The sodium content is typically under 50 mg per 100 g, roughly half of regular cottage cheese.
It is rich in casein, a slow‑digesting protein that supports muscle maintenance.
In some countries the product is called “cottage cheese,” although traditional Russian tvorog is produced differently.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Provides about 12–14 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, helping to preserve lean muscle mass.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Contains less than 1 g of fat per 100 g, making it ideal for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Delivers roughly 10–15 % of the daily calcium requirement, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt helps manage blood pressure and reduces kidney load.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consuming cottage cheese.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can cause skin rashes, swelling, or even anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although low, individuals on strict sodium restriction should still check the label.

items.title: Quality control
items.content: Improper storage can allow pathogenic bacteria to grow, so observe expiration dates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it plain, add to salads, blend into smoothies, use as a filling for pancakes or dumplings, or create low‑calorie desserts with fresh fruit or berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cottage cheese refrigerated at 0–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. It stays fresh for 5–7 days after opening. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

coffee-decaffeinated-pre-lightened-and-p.title: Decaffeinated Coffee, pre-lightened and pre-sweetened with sugar

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated Coffee, pre-lightened and pre-sweetened with sugar (5214) is a ground coffee from which almost all caffeine has been removed, then lightly roasted and sweetened with sugar for a smoother taste. Ideal for those who want the coffee aroma without the stimulating effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed with water or solvents while preserving most flavor compounds.
A light roast retains brighter fruity notes compared to a dark roast.
Adding sugar creates a sweeter beverage without artificial sweeteners.
Decaf coffee is often used in diets that limit caffeine intake.
The sugar helps balance the natural bitterness of coffee.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Even without caffeine, coffee retains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Certain coffee compounds can boost metabolic rate even in decaf form.

items.title: May reduce risk of some diseases
items.content: Regular moderate consumption of decaf coffee is linked to lower risk of type 2 diabetes and liver disease.

items.title: Provides energy without stimulation
items.content: Sugar offers a quick energy source, while coffee aroma can improve mood.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee contains small amounts of vitamins B2 and B3, supporting nervous system health.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The added sugar can raise blood glucose levels, so people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coffee components.

items.title: Residual caffeine
items.content: Decaf coffee still contains trace amounts of caffeine, which may affect highly caffeine‑sensitive persons.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can increase stomach acidity, causing discomfort for those with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 tsp of ground coffee into 180‑200 ml of hot (not boiling) water, let steep for 3‑4 minutes, then filter. Add milk, cream, or extra sweeteners to taste if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to preserve aroma and prevent oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Crackers are dry, crunchy baked goods often made from wheat or rice flour. Wonton are thin sheets of dough traditionally used in Asian cuisine for fillings and boiling. Both products are popular as quick snacks and as ingredients in various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers can be sweet or savory, with seeds, spices or cheese added.
Wonton originated in China over 2,000 years ago as a method to preserve meat.
In some countries wonton is served in soups, while in others it is fried to a crisp.
Crackers are frequently used as a base for canapés and fusion appetizers.
Wonton dough is typically unleavened, keeping the sheets elastic and easy to fold.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most cracker varieties are baked without large amounts of oil, making them a light snack.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Whole‑grain crackers provide slowly digestible carbohydrates that help sustain energy levels.

items.title: Protein boost with fillings
items.content: Wonton are often stuffed with meat, seafood or tofu, increasing the protein content of the dish.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat‑based dough supplies B1, B2 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Thin wonton sheets cook quickly, making them suitable for diets that limit heavy foods.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Savory crackers can be high in salt, which is undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crackers and wheat‑based wonton are not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some recipes include nuts, soy sauce or seafood, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Calorie density with toppings
items.content: Crackers topped with cheese or butter can become calorie‑rich and contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, paired with cheese, pâté, hummus, or used as a base for canapés. Wonton are boiled in broth, deep‑fried, or steamed with fillings such as meat, vegetables or tofu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place to keep them crisp. Keep wonton wrapped in plastic film in the refrigerator and use within a few days, or freeze for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Haddock is a cold‑water marine fish of the cod family, found in the North Atlantic. Fried haddock is made from fillets that are breaded and deep‑fried until golden and crisp. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a flaky texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Haddock is one of the most popular fish in the United Kingdom and Canada.
It provides more protein per calorie than most other seafood.
Wild haddock can grow up to 1 m, but commercial fillets usually come from fish 30–50 cm long.
Traditional dishes include “fish and chips” and smoked haddock (Finnan haddie).
Haddock migrates long distances during spawning, often traveling hundreds of kilometers.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of fried haddock supplies about 20 g of complete protein for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When fried with a moderate amount of oil, haddock remains relatively low‑calorie compared with many meats.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Haddock is rich in vitamin B12, niacin and B6, which support nervous system function and energy metabolism.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: The fish provides selenium, iodine and phosphorus, important for thyroid health and bone strength.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Although lower than fatty fish, haddock still contributes EPA and DHA omega‑3s that benefit heart health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including haddock.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Haddock is classified as low‑mercury fish, but excessive consumption should still be balanced with other protein sources.

items.title: Frying oil quality
items.content: High frying temperatures can produce trans fats; use oils with a high smoke point such as canola or sunflower.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Breaded and fried preparations often contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried haddock hot, with lemon wedges, tartar sauce, or malt vinegar. It works well in fish tacos, salads, sandwiches, or as a standalone main dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried haddock in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf made with beef is a baked dish prepared from ground beef, eggs, breadcrumbs, onion, and seasonings. It has a dense yet tender texture and a rich meaty flavor, often served in sliceable portions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the loaf is baked in a loaf pan, giving it a bread‑like shape.
In the United States it is commonly topped with a tomato‑based glaze or barbecue sauce.
The recipe dates back to the 19th century as a way to stretch meat with breadcrumbs.
Some regional variations add cheese, vegetables, or mushrooms for extra flavor.
Meat loaf slices store well, making it a popular choice for school lunches and picnics.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ground beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is readily absorbed and supports oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates offers lasting satiety.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Large amounts of beef can raise cholesterol levels, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Some recipes use a lot of salt or pre‑made sauces, increasing sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If breadcrumbs made from wheat are used, the dish is not suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Food‑borne bacteria risk
items.content: Improper cooking may leave the meat undercooked; ensure the internal temperature reaches 71 °C (160 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the meat loaf hot or cold, sliced thinly. It can be eaten on its own, in sandwiches, with vegetable sides, mashed potatoes, or salads. It pairs well with tomato sauce, mustard, or a honey‑mustard glaze.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked loaf to room temperature, then wrap tightly in plastic wrap or place in an airtight container. Refrigerate for up to 4 days. For longer storage, slice and freeze portions – they keep well for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 71 °C before serving.

meat-loaf-with-potatoes-vegetable-frozen.title: Meat loaf with potatoes, vegetable, frozen meal

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf with potatoes and vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal that combines a seasoned beef‑pork loaf with boiled potatoes and a mix of carrots, peas and corn. It is designed for quick reheating in a microwave or oven.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat loaf originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover meat.
Flash‑freezing preserves most nutrients while extending shelf life.
The combination of meat, potatoes and vegetables provides a balanced mix of protein, carbs and fiber.
Typical seasoning includes black pepper, paprika and a small amount of vegetable oil for flavor.
Packaging is usually multi‑layered to prevent freezer burn and maintain freshness.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat loaf supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and pork provide vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes and vegetables add potassium and magnesium, important for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetable blend contributes fiber that aids regular digestion.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: The meal contains little to no added sugar, making it suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Frozen ready meals often contain higher salt levels; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: To extend shelf life, some preservatives may be used, which can be unsuitable for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A minority of people may be allergic to beef or pork.

items.title: Heating requirements
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave harmful bacteria; follow the recommended temperature and time.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave (typically 3–4 minutes) or in an oven at 180 °C until the top is golden. Serve hot, optionally garnish with fresh herbs or a sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and store in the refrigerator at +2–4 °C.
